decks.title: Microbes in Human Welfare — Part 1: Microbes in the home and in industry
goals: Give examples of microbes used to make household foods
Name microbes used to produce beverages, antibiotics, acids and enzymes
Describe bioactive molecules such as streptokinase, cyclosporin A and statins

slides.heading: Microbes in Human Welfare
slides.body_md: Part 1 — microbes are not only germs: many make our food, drinks, medicines and industrial chemicals.

visual.alt: Flow of uses of microbes from household foods to industrial bioactive molecules

slides.narration: Microbes are everywhere, in soil, water and air, and inside our bodies. Some cause disease, but many are extremely useful. People have used microbes to make curd, bread and idli for thousands of years, and today industries use them to make medicines, chemicals and enzymes on a huge scale.

slides.heading: Microbes in household products
slides.body_md: Fermentation by microbes changes the taste, texture and nutrition of foods.

rows: Produce acids that coagulate and partly digest milk proteins; increase vitamin B₁₂; check disease-causing microbes in the stomach
Fermentation releases CO₂, which puffs up the dough
Fermentation releases CO₂ that makes the dough rise
Ferment the sap into a traditional drink

visual.alt: Table of household products with the microbes that make them

slides.narration: A spoonful of curd added to warm milk contains millions of lactic acid bacteria. They make acids that set the milk into curd and add vitamin B twelve. Dosa and idli batter rises overnight because bacteria release carbon dioxide; bread rises because of yeast. Even the holes in Swiss cheese are made by a bacterium releasing gas.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: what makes the dough rise?
slides.body_md: Two bowls of bread dough are kept warm. Bowl A has yeast; bowl B has no yeast. After two hours, only A has risen. A third bowl C has yeast but is kept in a refrigerator; it rises very little. Explain.
bullets: Step 1 — Only the bowls with **yeast** can ferment sugars, so the yeast causes the rise (A vs B).
Step 2 — Yeast releases **CO₂** during fermentation; the gas is trapped in the dough, which puffs up.
Step 3 — Fermentation is an **enzyme-driven** process that slows down at low temperature, so C rises little.
Conclusion — a living microbe, working best at a suitable temperature, raises the dough.

visual.alt: Worked table: dough rises only with yeast and warmth

slides.narration: Compare the bowls in pairs. A and B differ only in yeast, so yeast is needed. A and C differ only in temperature, so warmth is needed too. This is a controlled experiment, and it shows that the rising is caused by living yeast cells fermenting sugar and releasing carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Quick check: curd
slides.body_md: Which microbes convert milk into curd?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the acid these bacteria make.

slides.heading: Fermented beverages
slides.body_md: **Brewer’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)** ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to produce **ethanol**. Different raw materials and processing give different beverages.

visual.alt: Table of beverages made with and without distillation

slides.narration: The same yeast used in bread is used in industry to ferment sugars from grains and fruits into ethanol. Some drinks are bottled straight after fermentation, while others are distilled to concentrate the alcohol. We study this as an industrial process; alcohol itself is harmful to health, especially for young people.

slides.heading: Antibiotics: the story of penicillin
slides.body_md: **Antibiotics** are chemicals made by some microbes that kill or retard the growth of other, disease-causing microbes. **Alexander Fleming** noticed that a mould, **Penicillium notatum**, growing on a culture of **Staphylococci** stopped the bacteria from growing around it. **Ernst Chain and Howard Florey** later established its full potential as an antibiotic.

nodes.label: Clear zone: bacteria cannot grow near the mould
Mass production; used to treat wounded soldiers in World War II

visual.alt: Flow of the discovery and development of penicillin

slides.narration: Fleming’s observation was an accident: a mould spoiled one of his bacterial plates, but around the mould no bacteria grew. He identified the chemical responsible and named it penicillin. Chain and Florey purified it and proved its value, and it saved countless soldiers in the Second World War. Antibiotics have since greatly reduced deaths from plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.

slides.heading: Organic acids and enzymes
slides.body_md: Microbes are used to manufacture chemicals and enzymes in industry.

visual.alt: Table of organic acids and enzymes made by microbes with their uses

slides.narration: Fungi and bacteria are tiny chemical factories. A fungus makes citric acid, bacteria make acetic, butyric and lactic acids, and yeast makes ethanol. Microbial enzymes are useful too: lipases in detergents break down oily stains, and pectinases and proteases make fruit juices clear instead of cloudy.

slides.heading: Quick check: citric acid
slides.body_md: Which microbe is used for the commercial production of citric acid?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a fungus.

slides.heading: Bioactive molecules
slides.body_md: Some microbial products act as powerful medicines.

rows: “Clot buster”: removes clots from blood vessels of patients who have had a myocardial infarction (heart attack)
Lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting an enzyme of cholesterol synthesis

visual.alt: Table of bioactive molecules, the microbes that make them and their uses

slides.narration: Streptokinase from a bacterium dissolves blood clots in heart-attack patients. Cyclosporin A from a fungus suppresses the immune system so that a transplanted organ is not rejected. Statins from a yeast lower blood cholesterol by blocking an enzyme the body uses to make it. Each began as a molecule made by a microbe.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choosing the right microbial product
slides.body_md: Match each need to a microbial product, and name the microbe.
bullets: A patient has just had a heart attack caused by a blood clot → **streptokinase** (Streptococcus).
A patient has received a kidney transplant → **cyclosporin A** (Trichoderma polysporum), to prevent rejection.
A patient has very high blood cholesterol → **statins** (Monascus purpureus).
A detergent company wants to remove oily stains → **lipases**.

visual.alt: Worked table matching four needs to microbial products

slides.narration: Link each product to what it does. Streptokinase dissolves clots. Cyclosporin A suppresses immunity, which is exactly what a transplant patient needs. Statins block cholesterol synthesis. Lipases digest fats, which is why they work on oily stains. Learning the use with the product makes the microbe names easier to remember.

slides.heading: Quick check: penicillin
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about Fleming’s discovery.
slides.narration: Quick check. What did Fleming see around the mould?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Household: curd (lactic acid bacteria, vitamin B₁₂), dosa and idli (bacteria, CO₂), bread (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), toddy, cheese (Propionibacterium sharmanii for Swiss cheese).
Beverages: Saccharomyces cerevisiae; wine and beer without distillation; whisky, brandy and rum with distillation.
Antibiotics: penicillin from Penicillium notatum (Fleming; Chain and Florey).
Acids: citric (Aspergillus niger), acetic (Acetobacter aceti), butyric (Clostridium butylicum), lactic (Lactobacillus); ethanol (yeast). Enzymes: lipases, pectinases, proteases.
Bioactive molecules: streptokinase, cyclosporin A (Trichoderma polysporum), statins (Monascus purpureus).

visual.alt: Summary table of microbes and products

slides.narration: To recap: microbes make our curd, bread and cheese; ferment sugars into alcohol; give us antibiotics like penicillin; and produce acids, enzymes and medicines such as streptokinase, cyclosporin A and statins. Learn each microbe with its product and use.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn **microbe–product–use** as a triple.
Write scientific names correctly (genus capitalised).
For curd, mention **vitamin B₁₂** and protection in the stomach.
Know which drinks are **distilled**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn each microbe together with its product and use. Write scientific names carefully. For curd, mention vitamin B twelve and protection against harmful microbes. And remember which beverages are distilled.

goals: Describe primary and secondary treatment of sewage
Explain BOD and how it measures pollution
Describe the production of biogas and the role of methanogens

slides.heading: Microbes clean our water and give us fuel
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how microbes treat sewage, and how they produce biogas.

visual.alt: Flow from sewage through microbial treatment to cleaner water and biogas

slides.narration: Cities produce huge volumes of waste water, called sewage, full of organic matter and microbes, many of them pathogenic. It cannot be released directly into rivers. Sewage treatment plants use microbes themselves to clean it, and the leftover sludge can produce biogas, a useful fuel.

slides.heading: A sewage treatment plant
slides.body_md: Treatment happens in two stages: **primary** (physical) and **secondary** (biological).

visual.alt: Flow of a sewage treatment plant from primary to secondary treatment, settling tank, sludge digester and treated effluent

slides.narration: Follow the flow. First, solids are removed physically. Then the remaining liquid is treated by microbes in aeration tanks. The microbial flocs settle in a tank as activated sludge; some returns as a starter, and the rest goes to digesters that produce biogas. Finally, the cleaned effluent is released into a river.

slides.heading: Primary treatment
slides.body_md: **Primary treatment** is the physical removal of particles. Floating debris is removed by **sequential filtration**; grit (soil and small pebbles) is removed by **sedimentation**. The settled solids form **primary sludge**; the liquid above is the **effluent**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps of primary sewage treatment

slides.narration: Primary treatment works like a sieve and a settling pond. Large floating objects are filtered out, and heavy particles sink to the bottom. What sinks is primary sludge; the liquid that remains, the effluent, still contains a lot of dissolved organic matter and goes on to secondary treatment.

slides.heading: Secondary (biological) treatment
slides.body_md: The effluent is passed into large **aeration tanks** and agitated mechanically while air is pumped in. Useful **aerobic microbes** grow into **flocs** (masses of bacteria with fungal filaments) and consume most of the organic matter, greatly reducing the **BOD**.

nodes.label: Aeration tank: aerobic microbes form flocs
Settling tank: flocs settle as activated sludge
Small part returned to aeration tank as inoculum
Most sludge pumped to anaerobic digesters

visual.alt: Flow of secondary treatment from aeration tanks through settling to inoculum and digesters

slides.narration: Pumping in air lets aerobic bacteria and fungi flourish. They clump into flocs and feed on the dissolved organic matter, cleaning the water. When the BOD has fallen enough, the liquid is moved to a settling tank, where the flocs sink as activated sludge. A little sludge is recycled as a starter culture; the rest is digested anaerobically.

slides.heading: BOD: measuring organic pollution
slides.body_md: **BOD (biochemical oxygen demand)** is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in **one litre of water** were oxidised by bacteria. The **greater the BOD**, the **more polluted** the water with organic matter.

slides.narration: BOD tells us how much food for bacteria the water contains. Bacteria use oxygen as they break down organic matter, so more organic matter means more oxygen used. Untreated sewage has a high BOD; after secondary treatment it is much lower. High-BOD water released into rivers would use up the oxygen that fish need.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much does treatment help?
slides.body_md: Using the model values (BOD 300, 200, 30 mg per litre for raw sewage, after primary and after secondary treatment), find the percentage fall in BOD after primary treatment and after the whole treatment. How much oxygen would bacteria use in 1000 litres before and after treatment?
bullets: Step 1 — Primary: $\dfrac{300 - 200}{300} \times 100 \approx 33.3$ percent.
Step 2 — Overall: $\dfrac{300 - 30}{300} \times 100 = 90$ percent.
Step 3 — Oxygen in 1000 L: raw $300 \times 1000\ \text{mg} = 300\ \text{g}$; treated $30 \times 1000\ \text{mg} = 30\ \text{g}$.

visual.alt: Worked table: BOD falls 33.3 percent after primary and 90 percent overall

slides.narration: Primary treatment removes about a third of the BOD, because it removes only particles. Secondary treatment does most of the work, bringing the overall fall to ninety percent. In terms of oxygen, a thousand litres of raw sewage would use three hundred grams, but treated effluent only thirty grams, which a river can handle.

slides.heading: Anaerobic sludge digestion and clean rivers
slides.body_md: In **anaerobic sludge digesters**, other bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi of the sludge, producing a mixture of gases — **methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide** — that forms **biogas**. The treated effluent is released into rivers. The Ministry of Environment and Forests began the **Ganga Action Plan** and **Yamuna Action Plan** to build STPs and stop untreated sewage entering rivers.

rows: Treat sewage before it enters the Ganga
Treat sewage before it enters the Yamuna

visual.alt: Table of two river-cleaning programmes and their aims

slides.narration: Even the sludge is useful. In closed tanks without air, anaerobic bacteria break it down and release biogas, which can be used as fuel. Building enough treatment plants is a huge task, so national programmes like the Ganga and Yamuna Action Plans aim to treat sewage before it reaches our great rivers.

slides.heading: Biogas plants
slides.body_md: **Biogas** is mainly **methane**. **Methanogens** such as **Methanobacterium** grow anaerobically on cellulose material and produce methane, with CO₂ and H₂. They are found in anaerobic sludge and in the **rumen** of cattle, so cattle dung (gobar) is rich in them. The technology for rural biogas plants was developed in India by **IARI** and **KVIC**.

slides.narration: A biogas plant is a deep concrete tank fed with a slurry of dung and water. Methanogens digest it without air, producing gas that collects under a floating cover. The cover rises as gas builds up, and the gas is piped out for cooking and lighting. The leftover slurry is an excellent fertiliser.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: why put dung in a biogas plant?
slides.body_md: A village uses cattle dung either as dried cakes for burning or in a biogas plant. Compare the two uses.
bullets: Step 1 — Dung is rich in **methanogens** from the cattle rumen and in cellulose.
Step 2 — In a biogas plant, methanogens produce **methane-rich biogas**, a cleaner fuel for cooking and lighting.
Step 3 — The **spent slurry** is returned to fields as **fertiliser**.
Conclusion — the biogas plant gives fuel **and** fertiliser, and less smoke indoors than burning dung cakes.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing dung cakes with a biogas plant

slides.narration: Burning dung cakes gives heat but wastes the nutrients and fills homes with smoke. In a biogas plant, microbes turn the dung into a clean-burning gas, and the slurry still goes back to the fields as manure. So one material gives two benefits, which is why biogas plants are encouraged in rural areas.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Primary treatment: filtration and sedimentation; primary sludge and effluent.
Secondary treatment: aeration tanks, aerobic microbes form flocs, BOD falls; settling tank gives activated sludge; part returned as inoculum.
BOD: oxygen consumed if all organic matter in 1 litre were oxidised by bacteria; higher BOD = more polluted.
Anaerobic sludge digesters produce biogas (methane, H₂S, CO₂). Ganga and Yamuna Action Plans.
Biogas: methanogens (Methanobacterium) in sludge and cattle rumen; dung biogas plants (IARI, KVIC); slurry as fertiliser.

slides.heading: Microbes for greener farming
slides.body_md: Part 3 — using living organisms instead of chemicals to protect crops and enrich soil, and using antibiotics wisely.

nodes.label: Pollution and harm to useful organisms

visual.alt: Flow from chemical inputs and their problems to biological alternatives and organic farming

slides.narration: Chemical pesticides and fertilisers raise yields, but overuse pollutes soil and water and kills useful organisms. Biological methods use living organisms, often microbes, to control pests and supply nutrients. This is the basis of organic farming, which aims to keep the farm a healthy, balanced ecosystem.

slides.heading: Biological control of pests
slides.body_md: **Biocontrol** uses biological methods to control plant diseases and pests. The organic farmer aims not to eradicate every “pest” but to keep them at manageable levels within a **balanced ecosystem**.

rows: Several plant pathogens in the root zone

visual.alt: Table of biocontrol agents and the pests they control

slides.narration: Nature has its own pest controllers. Ladybirds eat aphids and dragonflies eat mosquitoes. Spores of the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis are sprayed on plants; caterpillars that eat them are killed by a toxin released in their gut, while other insects are spared. The fungus Trichoderma protects roots from disease.

slides.heading: Why narrow-spectrum control is better
slides.body_md: **Baculoviruses** are **species-specific, narrow-spectrum** insecticides with **no negative impact** on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even non-target insects. They suit **integrated pest management (IPM)**, especially in ecologically sensitive areas.

rows: Toxic residues in soil, water and food
Pests may return with no natural enemies

visual.alt: Table comparing broad-spectrum pesticides with narrow-spectrum biocontrol

slides.narration: A broad chemical spray kills the pest, but also the ladybirds, bees and other useful insects. With no natural enemies left, the pest can bounce back. Narrow-spectrum agents like baculoviruses attack only the target, so the rest of the ecosystem, including the pest’s natural enemies, stays intact.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: comparing pest control in two fields
slides.body_md: In two cotton fields, farmer A sprays a chemical insecticide 8 times a season; farmer B uses Bt spores and protects ladybirds and needs only 3 sprays of any kind. By what percentage has B reduced spraying, and what other benefits might follow?
bullets: Step 1 — Reduction $= \dfrac{8 - 3}{8} \times 100 \approx 62.5$ percent.
Step 2 — Fewer chemical sprays mean fewer residues in soil, water and food, and lower cost.
Step 3 — Natural enemies such as ladybirds survive and keep pests in check.

visual.alt: Worked table: spraying reduced by about 62.5 percent

slides.narration: Farmer B sprays five fewer times, about sixty-three percent less. The benefits go beyond cost: less chemical in the environment and in food, and a farm where useful predators thrive. Over several seasons, a balanced field often needs fewer interventions.

slides.heading: Quick check: Bt
slides.body_md: Which biocontrol agent is used to control butterfly caterpillars?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a bacterium whose spores are sprayed on plants.

slides.heading: Biofertilisers
slides.body_md: **Biofertilisers** are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. The main sources are **bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria**.

rows: Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes
Fix atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms
Absorb phosphorus for the plant; give resistance to root pathogens, salinity and drought
Fix nitrogen, especially in paddy fields; add organic matter

visual.alt: Table of biofertilisers with examples and how they help

slides.narration: Rhizobium bacteria live in nodules on the roots of pea, gram and other legumes and fix nitrogen from the air. Azotobacter and Azospirillum do the same while living freely in soil. Mycorrhizal fungi such as Glomus help roots absorb phosphorus and resist disease and drought. In rice fields, cyanobacteria fix nitrogen and add organic matter.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: does the biofertiliser work?
slides.body_md: A cooperative of 40 paddy farmers began adding cyanobacterial biofertiliser. Average yield rose from 2.5 to 3 tonnes per hectare. Find the percentage increase and suggest a reason.
bullets: Step 1 — Increase $= \dfrac{3 - 2.5}{2.5} \times 100 = 20$ percent.
Step 2 — Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena and Nostoc **fix atmospheric nitrogen** in the flooded fields and add **organic matter**.
Caution — other factors (weather, seed) may also differ between years; a fair test needs control plots without biofertiliser.

visual.alt: Worked table: yield rose 20 percent

slides.narration: Half a tonne extra on two and a half is a twenty percent increase. Cyanobacteria are well suited to paddy fields because they thrive in standing water and fix nitrogen. A careful scientist would still compare with control plots, because yields also depend on rain, seeds and other conditions.

slides.heading: Quick check: mycorrhiza
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about mycorrhizae.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which nutrient does the fungus help the plant absorb?

slides.heading: Using antibiotics judiciously
slides.body_md: Antibiotics are among the greatest gifts of microbes, but **misuse** — taking them without prescription, for viral infections, or stopping the course early — selects **resistant bacteria**, which then spread.

rows: Use only when prescribed by a doctor
Antibiotics do not act on viruses such as those causing the common cold
Stopping early lets the toughest bacteria survive and multiply
Do not share or reuse old antibiotics
Wrong drug or dose encourages resistance
Resistant bacteria can pass to people

visual.alt: Table of good practices for antibiotic use with reasons

slides.narration: Every time antibiotics are used, sensitive bacteria die and the few resistant ones survive. Overuse speeds up this natural selection, and infections become harder to treat. So antibiotics must be used only when a doctor prescribes them, at the right dose, for the full course. They never cure viral illnesses like colds.

slides.heading: Quick check: antibiotic resistance
slides.body_md: Why does stopping a course of antibiotics early encourage resistance?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which bacteria are left alive when the course is cut short?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Biocontrol: ladybirds (aphids), dragonflies (mosquitoes), Bacillus thuringiensis (caterpillars), Trichoderma (root pathogens), baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus; narrow-spectrum, IPM).
Organic farming keeps pests at manageable levels in a balanced ecosystem.
Biofertilisers: Rhizobium (legume nodules), Azospirillum and Azotobacter (free-living), mycorrhiza (Glomus: phosphorus, resistance), cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria in paddy).
Judicious antibiotic use: only on prescription, full course, never for viral infections.

visual.alt: Summary table of biocontrol agents and biofertilisers

slides.narration: To recap: living organisms can control pests and diseases with little harm to the environment, and microbes can enrich soil with nitrogen and phosphorus. These are the foundations of organic farming. And antibiotics, our most valuable microbial products, must be used wisely to keep them working.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **one example for each type** of biocontrol agent and biofertiliser.
Explain **why** narrow-spectrum agents suit IPM.
State **two benefits of mycorrhiza** beyond phosphorus.
Link antibiotic misuse to **natural selection of resistance**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Have one example ready for each kind of biocontrol agent and biofertiliser. Explain the advantage of narrow-spectrum control. Remember the extra benefits of mycorrhiza. And explain antibiotic resistance as natural selection.

sections.heading: 1. Microbes in household products
sections.body_md:
- **Curd:** *Lactobacillus* and other **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)** grow in milk, produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins, **increase vitamin B₁₂**, and check disease-causing microbes in the stomach. A small amount of curd added to fresh milk acts as the inoculum.
- **Dosa and idli:** dough fermented by **bacteria**; CO₂ makes it puff up.
- **Bread:** dough fermented by **baker's yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*)**.
- **Toddy:** traditional drink made by fermenting palm sap.
- **Cheese:** large holes in **Swiss cheese** from CO₂ produced by ***Propionibacterium sharmanii***; **Roquefort cheese** ripened by specific fungi for flavour.

key_terms.definition_md: Breakdown of sugars by microbes, often without oxygen, producing acids, alcohol or gases.
A small quantity of microbes added to start a culture or fermentation.

visual.alt: Table of household products and microbes

sections.heading: 2. Microbes in industry
sections.body_md:
**Beverages:** brewer's yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to ethanol. **Wine and beer** are produced **without distillation**; **whisky, brandy and rum** by **distilling** the fermented broth.

**Antibiotics:** chemicals produced by some microbes that kill or retard the growth of disease-causing microbes. **Penicillin** — discovered by **Alexander Fleming** while working on *Staphylococci*: a mould, ***Penicillium notatum***, prevented their growth; its full potential was established by **Ernst Chain and Howard Florey**; used for wounded soldiers in World War II; Nobel Prize 1945. Antibiotics have greatly improved treatment of plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.

**Chemicals and enzymes:**
| Product | Microbe |
|---|---|
| Citric acid | *Aspergillus niger* (fungus) |
| Acetic acid | *Acetobacter aceti* (bacterium) |
| Butyric acid | *Clostridium butylicum* (bacterium) |
| Lactic acid | *Lactobacillus* (bacterium) |
| Ethanol | *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (yeast) |

**Lipases** in detergents remove oily stains; **pectinases and proteases** clarify bottled juices.

**Bioactive molecules:** **streptokinase** (from *Streptococcus*, modified by genetic engineering) — "clot buster" for patients who have had a myocardial infarction; **cyclosporin A** (from *Trichoderma polysporum*) — immunosuppressant for organ-transplant patients; **statins** (from the yeast *Monascus purpureus*) — lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting an enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.

key_terms.definition_md: A chemical produced by a microbe that kills or retards the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes.
Microbial products that lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting an enzyme of its synthesis.

sections.heading: 3. Sewage treatment
sections.body_md:
**Sewage** (municipal waste water) contains large amounts of organic matter and microbes, many pathogenic; it is treated in **sewage treatment plants (STPs)** before release into natural water bodies.

**Primary treatment** (physical): floating debris removed by sequential **filtration**; grit (soil, small pebbles) by **sedimentation**. Settled solids = **primary sludge**; supernatant = **effluent**.

**Secondary (biological) treatment:** effluent passed into large **aeration tanks**, agitated and pumped with air; useful aerobic microbes grow into **flocs** (bacteria associated with fungal filaments in mesh-like structures), which consume most of the organic matter, significantly reducing the **BOD**. Then the effluent goes to a **settling tank**, where flocs sediment as **activated sludge**; a small part is pumped back into the aeration tank as **inoculum**; the major part goes to **anaerobic sludge digesters**, where other bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi, producing **biogas** (methane, hydrogen sulphide, CO₂). The treated effluent is released into rivers.

**BOD (biochemical oxygen demand):** the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in **one litre of water** were oxidised by bacteria; **higher BOD = more polluting potential**.

The **Ministry of Environment and Forests** initiated the **Ganga Action Plan** and **Yamuna Action Plan** to save these rivers from pollution.

key_terms.definition_md: Oxygen that would be consumed if all organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria; a measure of organic pollution.
Masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments that form in aeration tanks.
Sediment of flocs in the settling tank; partly reused as inoculum.

sections.heading: 4. Biogas
sections.body_md:
**Biogas** is a mixture of gases, predominantly **methane**, produced by microbial activity; it is used as fuel. **Methanogens** such as ***Methanobacterium*** grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce large amounts of methane, with CO₂ and H₂. They occur in anaerobic sludge and in the **rumen** of cattle (where they help digest cellulose), so **cattle dung (gobar)** is rich in them.

**Biogas plant:** a concrete tank (10–15 feet deep) into which bio-wastes and a **slurry of dung** are fed; a **floating cover** over the slurry rises as gas is produced; an outlet pipe supplies gas for **cooking and lighting**; spent slurry is removed through another outlet and used as **fertiliser**. The technology was developed in India mainly by **IARI** (Indian Agricultural Research Institute) and **KVIC** (Khadi and Village Industries Commission).

key_terms.definition_md: Anaerobic microbes such as Methanobacterium that produce methane.
A fuel gas, mainly methane, produced by microbial digestion of organic matter.

sections.heading: 5. Biocontrol agents and biofertilisers; judicious use of antibiotics
sections.body_md:
**Biocontrol** uses biological methods to control plant diseases and pests, reducing dependence on chemicals that are toxic to humans and animals and pollute the environment. Organic farmers aim to keep pests at manageable levels through a balanced ecosystem.
- **Ladybird** beetles (aphids) and **dragonflies** (mosquitoes).
- ***Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt):** spores sprayed on plants; caterpillars that eat them are killed by a toxin released in their gut; other insects are unharmed.
- ***Trichoderma*:** free-living fungi in the root ecosystem; biocontrol of several plant pathogens.
- **Baculoviruses** (genus ***Nucleopolyhedrovirus***): species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticides with no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects; useful in **integrated pest management (IPM)**.

**Biofertilisers** enrich the nutrient quality of soil:
- **Rhizobium** — symbiotic in root nodules of leguminous plants; fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
- **Azospirillum, Azotobacter** — free-living nitrogen fixers in soil.
- **Mycorrhiza** (fungi of genus ***Glomus***) — absorb **phosphorus** from soil for the plant; also give resistance to root pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought.
- **Cyanobacteria** (***Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria***) — fix nitrogen, especially in **paddy fields**; add organic matter.

**Judicious use of antibiotics:** use only on prescription, at the correct dose, for the full course; never for viral infections; misuse selects resistant bacteria.

questions.stem_md: Describe the secondary (biological) treatment of sewage.

answer.model_answer_md:
The primary effluent is passed into large **aeration tanks**, where it is agitated mechanically and air is pumped in. Useful **aerobic microbes** grow into **flocs** (bacteria with fungal filaments) and consume most of the organic matter, **reducing the BOD** significantly.

The effluent then goes to a **settling tank**, where the flocs sediment as **activated sludge**. A small part is pumped back into the aeration tank as **inoculum**; most goes to **anaerobic sludge digesters**, where other bacteria digest it, producing **biogas**. The treated effluent is released into rivers.

questions.stem_md: Describe how sewage is treated in a sewage treatment plant. Explain the role of microbes and the significance of BOD in the process.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Why treat sewage.** Municipal waste water contains large amounts of organic matter and microbes, many of them pathogenic, and cannot be discharged directly into rivers.

**Primary treatment.** This is physical: floating debris is removed by sequential filtration, and grit is removed by sedimentation. The settled solids form primary sludge, and the liquid above, the effluent, goes to secondary treatment.

**Secondary treatment.** In aeration tanks the effluent is agitated and air is pumped in. Aerobic microbes grow into flocs, masses of bacteria with fungal filaments, and consume most of the organic matter, so the BOD falls sharply. BOD is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria, so it measures how polluting the water is. When the BOD is low enough, the effluent passes to a settling tank, where the flocs settle as activated sludge.

**Sludge.** A small part of the activated sludge is returned as inoculum; the rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, where bacteria digest it and produce biogas (methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide).

**Release.** The treated effluent is released into natural water bodies. Programmes such as the Ganga and Yamuna Action Plans aim to build enough plants to treat sewage before it reaches rivers.

questions.solution_md: Primary; secondary with flocs and BOD; sludge digestion; release.

questions.stem_md: What are biofertilisers? Give one example each of a bacterial, a fungal and a cyanobacterial biofertiliser and how it helps the plant.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Biofertilisers** are organisms that **enrich the nutrient quality of the soil**.

1. **Bacterial:** ***Rhizobium*** in root nodules of legumes **fixes atmospheric nitrogen** (Azotobacter and Azospirillum do so free-living).

2. **Fungal:** **mycorrhiza** (***Glomus***) **absorbs phosphorus** for the plant and gives resistance to root pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought.

questions.stem_md: What are biocontrol agents and biofertilisers? Explain, with examples, how each helps farmers reduce the use of chemicals.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Biocontrol agents** are living organisms used to control plant diseases and pests. Ladybird beetles eat aphids and dragonflies eat mosquitoes. Spores of Bacillus thuringiensis sprayed on plants kill caterpillars through a toxin released in their gut, without harming other insects. Free-living Trichoderma fungi in the root zone control several plant pathogens. Baculoviruses of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus are species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticides with no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects, so they suit integrated pest management. Using them reduces chemical pesticides that are toxic and pollute soil and water.

**Biofertilisers** are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of soil. Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes and free-living Azospirillum and Azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen. Mycorrhizal fungi such as Glomus absorb phosphorus for the plant and give resistance to root pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought. Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria fix nitrogen in paddy fields and add organic matter. Using them reduces the need for chemical fertilisers.

Together they form the basis of organic farming, which keeps pests at manageable levels within a balanced ecosystem.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; biocontrol examples; biofertiliser examples; reduced chemical use.

questions.stem_md: A farmers’ group is debating whether to replace all chemical pesticides and fertilisers with biocontrol agents and biofertilisers. Evaluate this proposal, giving its advantages, its limitations and a sensible recommendation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Advantages.** Biocontrol agents such as Bacillus thuringiensis, Trichoderma and baculoviruses are specific to pests or pathogens, so they spare useful insects, birds, fish and people, leave no toxic residues, and keep the natural enemies of pests alive. Biofertilisers such as Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Glomus and cyanobacteria add nitrogen or improve phosphorus uptake and organic matter, improving soil health over time and lowering costs. Together they reduce pollution of soil and water.

**Limitations.** Biological methods often act more slowly, need correct timing and conditions (living organisms must survive), and may not stop a sudden severe outbreak. Farmers need training, and quality supply of inoculants. Yields may dip during the changeover.

**Recommendation.** Rather than an immediate total switch, the group should adopt integrated pest management and integrated nutrient management: use biocontrol and biofertilisers as the first choice, monitor pests, and use chemicals only when necessary and in small amounts, gradually reducing them as the farm ecosystem becomes balanced.

**Judgement.** The proposal is sound in direction but should be phased in.

questions.solution_md: Advantages, limitations, phased IPM recommendation.

questions.stem_md: Explain what antibiotics are, using penicillin as an example, and describe five rules for using antibiotics judiciously, giving the reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Antibiotics** are chemical substances produced by some microbes that can kill or retard the growth of other, disease-causing microbes. Penicillin, made by the mould Penicillium notatum, was discovered by Alexander Fleming when he saw that Staphylococci could not grow around the mould; Chain and Florey later established it as a medicine, and it saved many lives in World War II.

**Judicious use.**
1. Take antibiotics only when prescribed by a doctor — self-medication may use the wrong drug.
2. Do not use them for viral infections such as colds — they act only on bacteria, and needless use selects resistance.
3. Take the correct dose at the right times — low doses let bacteria survive.
4. Complete the full course — stopping early leaves the most resistant bacteria alive to multiply.
5. Do not share or keep leftover antibiotics, and avoid unnecessary use in farm animals — both spread resistant bacteria.

These rules slow the natural selection of resistant bacteria, so that antibiotics keep working for everyone.

questions.solution_md: Definition, penicillin, five reasoned rules.
